Building Information Systems and the Business Case

Why organizations build systems, and how to show the investment is justified.

🎯 Learning outcome: justify the development of information systems using structured analysis.

🛠️ Case: Vinci Energies’ MOBITIME app

  • Vinci Energies: 82,000 employees, 55 countries; every cost tracked to a project.
  • Problem: field workers returned to the office just to enter data.
  • Solution: MOBITIME, an SAP Cloud app for time sheets and costs from anywhere.
  • Approach: analyze, redesign the process, design the UX, then build.
Discussion question 1: How did MOBITIME meet Vinci’s information requirements?Captures time and costs on site and ties them to the right project.
Discussion question 2: How did the new system change Vinci’s business operations?No trips back to the office: less time and cost, more direct cost tracking.

How systems produce organizational change

A new system changes how people work. The question: how much change, and at what risk?

DegreeWhat changesExampleReward and risk
1 · AutomationAssists employees with routine tasks.Paper time sheets become a mobile form; approvals stay the same.Lowest
2 · Rationalization of proceduresStreamlines procedures and removes bottlenecks.One online form replaces five request forms.Low
3 · Business process redesignReorganizes workflows and combines steps.MOBITIME removes the trip back to the office.High
4 · Paradigm shiftTransforms the nature of the business.A bookstore becomes an online retailer.Highest

Higher degrees of change offer greater potential rewards but carry greater risk.

Select a degree to compare its reward and risk.

Business process management (BPM)

1 · Identify

Pick the processes that need to change.

2 · Analyze

Study how the current processes work.

3 · Design

Create the new, improved processes.

4 · Implement

Put the new process into practice.

5 · Measure

Keep measuring performance continuously.

BPM tools: model processes, capture rules, integrate systems, measure performance. Example: BT Group (Pegasystems).

📚 Redesigning a process

Compare buying a book in a physical store with buying it online.

🎯 Justify it: start with the business challenge and an honest estimate of the change required.

Identifying Information Needs

Systems analysis

Analysis turns a vague problem into checkable requirements. Examples: a school canteen pre-order app.

🧩 Problem definition

Define the problem the system must solve.

Example: students lose break time in long canteen lines.

🔎 Cause identification

Find out what is causing it.

Example: orders are taken one at a time at the counter, and students only learn what has sold out when they reach the front.

✍️ Solution specification

Specify the solutions worth considering.

Example: a pre-order app, a second serving counter, or a ready-made ordering package.

📋 Information requirements

Identify who needs what information, where and when.

Example: students need the menu and a pickup time, staff need the order list, and the cashier needs payment confirmation.

⚖️ Feasibility study

Test whether the solution is feasible financially, technically and organizationally.

Example: can the school afford it, do student phones and school Wi-Fi support it, and will staff change how they take orders?

⚠️ Remember: faulty requirements are a leading cause of system failure.

Functional and non-functional requirements

Information requirements come in two kinds. Capturing both is how analysis avoids the faulty-requirements failures above.

⚙️ Functional: what the system must do

The tasks, features, inputs, processing and outputs users need, usually written as “a user can…” or “the system shall…”. Test: can you demonstrate it as a task?

📏 Non-functional: how well it must do it

Quality and constraints such as performance, usability, reliability, availability, security, compatibility and scalability. Test: can you measure it, for example “loads in under 3 seconds”?

Why both matter: a full-featured system still fails if slow, confusing, insecure or down. Functional → what to draw; non-functional → how to design and test.

From needs to wireframes

A low-fidelity wireframe is a quick sketch of screens in simple shapes, checked with users before anything is built.

1 · Requirements

Identify users, tasks and main features.

2 · User flow

List key screens and the navigation between them.

3 · Sketch

Use simple shapes: boxes, lines and circles.

4 · Components

Place only the necessary UI elements.

5 · Annotate

Label screen name, purpose and notes.

6 · Review

Check the design supports the tasks and objectives.

🎯 Justify it: clear needs and tested wireframes make costs and benefits easier to estimate.

Structured Analysis and Design

From what the system must do to how it will do it.

Core activities in systems development

1 · Systems analysis

Define the problem, identify its causes and specify solutions.

2 · Systems design

Create the specifications that will fulfill the requirements.

3 · Programming

Translate design specifications into code.

4 · Testing

Verify that the system produces the desired results.

5 · Conversion

Change over from the old system to the new one.

6 · Production and maintenance

Operate the system, correct errors and keep improving it.

Data flow diagrams (DFD)

A data flow diagram (DFD) shows how data moves between people, processes and files.

🔀 DFD: Student Enrollment

Four symbols: external entities (squares), processes (rounded boxes), data stores (open rectangles) and data flows (arrows). Select a type to highlight it.

See the textbook version of this diagram

Structured vs. object-oriented modeling

  • Structured: processes and data kept separate (employee data → compute pay → paycheck).
  • Object-oriented: data and operations bundled into objects and classes.
  • Inheritance: Salaried, Hourly and Temporary inherit from Employee, so objects are reused.

🧱 Two ways to model the same system

Switch views, then tap a subclass to see what it inherits (attributes are illustrative).

Design specifications

The model says what the system does; the design specifications say precisely how it will be built.

SpecificationSaysCanteen app example
User interfaceScreens and layouts (where wireframes feed in)Menu, cart and pickup-status screens
Data modelWhat data is kept and how it relatesStudent, Menu item, Order; one student places many orders
ProcessingThe logic of each processPlace order = check stock, total, confirm payment, issue pickup number
Input and outputWhat goes in and comes outSelections in; confirmation and daily sales report out
Hardware and networkEquipment and connectionsPhones, counter screen, school Wi-Fi, cloud hosting
Controls and securityProtections for accuracy and useLogin, protected payments, duplicate-order checks, activity log
👥 User involvement is critical so the design reflects business priorities.

Testing and conversion

Test at three levels, then convert using one of four strategies.

🧪 Three levels of testing

Unit: each program on its own. System: the whole system working together. Acceptance: final sign-off by users and management.

🔁 Four conversion strategies

Parallel: old and new run side by side (safest). Direct cutover: switch on a set date (riskiest). Pilot: one area first. Phased: one function or unit at a time.

Alternative ways to build

Each approach trades speed, cost and control differently.

ApproachHow it worksBest forWatch out for
Systems life cycleFormal phases; each finishes before the next; heavy documentation.Large, complex, well-defined systemsCostly and inflexible
PrototypingBuild a quick working model, let users try it, revise and repeat.Unclear requirementsMay skip essential steps
Software package / cloudBuy or subscribe to ready-made software.Speed, standard processesCustomization; adapting to the package
OutsourcingHire an outside firm, local or offshore.Skills and savingsHidden costs add 15% to 57% to offshore contracts
  • Fast-cycle methods: RAD, JAD (sessions with users), agile (small iterations), DevOps, low-code/no-code.
  • Mobile: mobile website, mobile web app or native app; responsive design fits every screen.
🎯 Justify it: the logical model lets each alternative be priced and compared.

System Justification: The Business Case

📖 The story: you are a Vinci analyst. Should management fund MOBITIME? Each step answers the approvers’ next question.
1 Worth solving?→2 Fits the plan?→3 Ranks well?→4 Best option?→5 Costs vs. benefits→6 Trust the numbers?→7 Recommend

1 · Is the problem worth solving? The business case

📄 Business case: a proposal for an investment covering problem, costs, benefits, risks, alternatives and required change.

Seven factors approvers check: new products and services · strategy · survival · financial rationale · customers and suppliers · IT plan fit · better decisions.

🧭 Business Case Explorer

Tap each factor around the hub to read the question approvers will ask. Each one is checked off automatically once you have reviewed it.

2 · Does it fit our plan? The information systems plan

The IS plan links IT to corporate goals: current systems, priorities, milestones, change, strategy and budget. A project that fits it is easier to approve.

3 · How does it rank against other projects? Portfolio analysis

  • Portfolio analysis lists every IS project and asset and weighs risk against benefit, like an investment portfolio.
  • No mix suits every industry.
  • Payoff: better return on IT, alignment with goals, coordination.
Low risk
High risk
High benefit
Priority projectsFund and develop first
Second priority, carefully managedProceed, but manage the risk
Low benefit
Candidates for replacementConsider replacing
AvoidDo not pursue

Greener cells are more attractive; redder cells are less attractive. Risk rises left to right, and benefit falls top to bottom.

4 · Which option is best? Scoring models

A scoring model weights each criterion and totals the scores, making priorities explicit and the choice transparent.

🧮 Weighted Scoring Model

Two alternatives are scored on four criteria (scores are illustrative). Change the weights and watch the winner.

5 · What will it cost, and what will we get? Costs and benefits

💸 Information system costs

  • Hardware and software acquisition
  • Telecommunications
  • Personnel and training
  • Facility costs
  • Consultant fees
  • Software upgrades and maintenance

Total cost of ownership (TCO) adds them all up.

🎁 Benefits

Tangible (can be valued in money): cost reduction, productivity, increased sales, lower inventory costs.

Intangible (not immediately quantifiable): better customer service, better decisions, higher morale.

🧾 Capital Budgeting Calculator

Enter illustrative figures to compare payback, ROI, NPV and IRR.

6 · Can we trust the numbers? Limits of financial models

⚠️ Watch out: financial models miss disruption, training and productivity dips, and undervalue intangibles. Pair them with the risk and portfolio views.

7 · Write the recommendation

Problem→Plan fit→Portfolio position→Best option→Costs and benefits→Risks and limits

Risks and Project Management

📖 The story: MOBITIME is approved. Next: what can go wrong, how risky it is, the people side, and staying on track.
1 What goes wrong?→2 What we manage→3 How risky?→4 People→5 Plan and control→6 Success

1 · What goes wrong? Why projects fail

66%

average budget overrun on large projects

33%

average schedule overrun on large projects

70%

failure rate reported for business process management projects

>50%

of businesses experience IT project failure every year

Failure looks like: over budget, late, underperforming, or unused (staff keep manual records). Runaway projects underestimate budget and time by 50% or more.

2 · What are we managing? Five project variables

Project management applies knowledge, skills, tools and techniques to hit targets within constraints.

📐 Scope

What work is, and is not, included.

⏱️ Time

How long the work will take.

💵 Cost

The budget for resources and expenses.

🏅 Quality

How well the results meet the objectives.

⚠️ Risk

The problems that could threaten success.

Managing them: plan, assess risk, estimate and acquire resources, assign tasks, control, report and review.

3 · How risky is this project? Risk dimensions

  • Project size
    • Measured by budget, staff, timeline and the number of organizational units affected
    • Larger projects have 50 to 75% higher failure rates
  • Project structure
    • Defined requirements, clear outputs and user agreement lower the risk
    • Fluid, undefined requirements raise it
  • Technical expertise
    • Depends on the team’s hardware, software and database expertise
    • A steep learning curve increases the risk

🎚️ Risk Assessor

Switch each dimension to describe the project and see its risk level.

Project size
Requirements
Technology

Managing risk: fit tools to the risk. Complex technology → experienced team, frequent meetings, outside experts, prototypes. BPM (~70% fail), enterprise apps and mergers carry extra risk.

4 · What about the people? Change management

People factorWhat it means
Management supportThe most critical success factor: it secures funding and priority and enforces change.
User involvementUsers as active team members get the design right and accept the result.
Communications gapUsers and designers differ in priorities and vocabulary; the analyst acts as change agent.
ResistanceCounterimplementation is deliberate action to block a system. Answer it with participation, training, incentives, management policy and friendlier interfaces.
Organizational impactPlan for effects on jobs, power, ergonomics, morale and training; sociotechnical design balances technical and human needs.

5 · How do we keep it on track? Planning and control

Gantt charts list activities with start and finish dates and show timing and duration.

PERT charts show task dependencies, so you can find the critical path.

Project management software (such as Microsoft Project) builds these charts and tracks progress automatically.

📅 Gantt Chart Explorer: HRIS Data Administration Project

Highlight, tap a task, or filter by person. Months are approximate.

🕸️ PERT Explorer: Small Website Project

Pick a view, tap a task, or change a duration (days) to see whether the critical path moves. On a phone, scroll the diagram sideways.

6 · What makes it succeed?

✅ Success factors

A business case aligned with strategy, effective project management, user involvement, management support, attention to organizational impact, and appropriate tools and methodologies.

💡 Remember

IS projects are business investments. Manage risk continuously; organizational change matters as much as technical change.

🎯 Justify it: show the risks and how you will manage them, or the benefit estimates won’t be trusted.

Key takeaways

🔄 Planned change

Systems development is planned organizational change.

🧭 Structured process

Development follows distinct activities and draws on several modeling methods.

🧰 Many ways to build

Teams can choose among the life cycle, prototyping, software packages and outsourcing.

💼 A business investment

A system is a business investment, so it needs a business case aligned with strategy.

🤝 People matter

Success depends on user involvement and on management support.

⚡ Agility

Modern development favors speed, small steps and constant feedback.

✏️ Sketch first

Low-fidelity wireframes make requirements visible early and cheaply, before anything is built.

Review questions
